strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in patch-token world-model planning: repeated transformer rollouts during MPC are computationally expensive.

The proposed combination of random token dropping and randomized grouped-attention training is simple, intuitive, and produces substantial measured wall-clock reductions, often retaining competitive success rates at moderate drop ratios.
The evaluation covers six visually and dynamically diverse simulated control environments, including navigation, rigid-object manipulation, and deformable-object manipulation.
The paper includes useful comparisons with a full-patch model, a CLS-token model, several learned or attention-based token-selection methods, spatial sampling, fixed masks, and token clustering.

Ablations and diagnostic analyses investigate grouped attention, prediction error, state information in retained tokens, probing performance, mask resampling, and robustness of CEM to synthetic noise.
The method exposes a straightforward accuracy-efficiency tradeoff through the drop ratio and appears easy to implement.
weaknesses: The main technical idea is fairly incremental: random patch dropout is well established, and the paper primarily adapts it to transformer world-model rollouts with a grouped-attention training scheme. The novelty relative to prior token sparsification and dropout methods is therefore limited.

Several central claims are overstated. The method is described as adaptive, but the dropout ratio is manually selected rather than adapted online. The claim of seamless integration with any transformer world model conflicts with the need for specialized grouped-attention training. The paper also incorrectly states that computation scales exponentially with the number of visual tokens, whereas standard self-attention scales quadratically.

The real-time motivation is not convincingly supported. Reported planning times remain extremely large—tens to hundreds of seconds per iteration—and there is no real-time or real-robot demonstration. Timing methodology, batching, hardware utilization, variance, FLOPs, memory consumption, and end-to-end control frequency are insufficiently documented.

Success-rate estimates use only 20–60 trials and are reported without confidence intervals, seeds, or significance tests. Many claimed improvements over the full-patch model are small enough to plausibly reflect sampling noise, especially on the 20- and 30-episode datasets.

The assertion that sophisticated selection methods are not significantly better than random sampling is unsupported by statistical testing. Table 3 further averages results over dropout ratios, potentially obscuring important accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs, and contains missing evaluations for multiple baselines.

Baseline comparability is unclear. The full-patch baseline is described as using positional encodings, while the exact architectural and training differences from the proposed grouped-attention model are not fully controlled. Consequently, performance gains cannot be cleanly attributed to sparse imagination rather than training regularization or implementation differences.

The experiments are confined to simulated benchmarks, largely inherited from one prior world-model setup, with one visual encoder and limited environment diversity relative to the broad robotics and deployment claims. There is no comparison to alternative efficient world-model architectures, reduced-resolution/token-grid models, or matched-compute smaller transformers.

The robustness explanation is weak: absence of visible structure in a two-dimensional UMAP plot does not justify modeling prediction errors as independent zero-mean Gaussian noise. The subsequent synthetic-noise experiment therefore does not establish robustness to the actual structured errors induced by token dropping.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous, including when masks are resampled, whether identical masks are used for observations, goals, candidates, and rollout steps, and how timing is measured. There are also inconsistencies between the main text and appendix regarding MPC iteration limits and whether complete planned sequences are executed, which impair reproducibility.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical bottleneck: transformer world-model rollouts can be prohibitively expensive for model-predictive control.
The proposed combination of random patch dropping and randomized grouped attention is simple, easy to understand, and exposes a useful user-controlled accuracy–cost trade-off.
Evaluation covers six simulated control environments with different dynamics, and reports results over a broad range of dropout ratios rather than a single favorable setting.
The paper includes useful comparisons with several token-selection and token-merging strategies, as well as ablations on grouped attention and measurements of planning time.
The appendix provides substantial implementation detail and additional prediction-error, noise-robustness, and runtime experiments.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited. Patch dropout and masked/grouped attention are established ideas, and their application to a DINO-feature world model is an incremental extension without a new learning principle, theoretical result, or adaptive allocation mechanism. Despite the abstract's wording, the dropout ratio is manually chosen rather than adaptively determined from computational resources.

The evaluation does not support the strong real-time deployment claims. Even sparse configurations require roughly 42–278 seconds per reported planning iteration, and the paper does not demonstrate real-time control, latency on constrained robotic hardware, or any physical-robot experiment.

The success-rate evidence lacks uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, seed-level results, and statistical tests. Sample sizes are as low as 20 episodes, while ten dropout ratios are examined and favorable maxima are emphasized. Several apparent improvements over the full model could therefore be sampling noise or post-hoc ratio selection.

The baselines are insufficient for a top-tier efficiency paper. The main comparisons are only full-patch and CLS-token variants of the same framework. There are no competitive efficient world-model or planning baselines, compute-matched alternatives, or comparisons with reduced model width/depth, lower-resolution features, fewer CEM candidates, or shorter planning horizons.

The full-patch comparison is not clearly controlled. The paper indicates differences involving grouped versus full attention and positional encoding, but does not cleanly report a p=0 counterpart of the proposed trained model. Consequently, performance differences can be confounded by training regularization or architecture rather than sparse imagination itself.

Claims that sophisticated selection methods are not significantly better than random sampling are unsupported by significance tests. Table 3 averages performance across dropout ratios, obscuring the accuracy–compute frontier, and many competing-method entries are missing on some environments.

The supporting analyses are methodologically weak. nHSIC is repeatedly described as mutual information even though it is a dependence measure, and comparisons across representations with different token counts may be dimension-sensitive. The probe predicts only four coarse particle-distribution statistics, which does not establish preservation of task-relevant fine-grained state.

The robustness argument is particularly unconvincing: absence of an obvious pattern in a two-dimensional UMAP visualization does not justify modeling actual prediction errors as independent zero-mean Gaussian noise. Experiments with synthetic Gaussian perturbations therefore do not validate robustness to the structured errors produced by token dropping.

Several technical statements and protocol descriptions are inaccurate or ambiguous. Attention cost is quadratic, not exponential, in token count; it is unclear precisely when masks are resampled and whether candidates share a mask; and the appendix says the entire planned action sequence is executed at each MPC step, which conflicts with the stated receding-horizon formulation.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the appendix: there is no stated release of the proposed implementation or trained models, important environment-specific planning details and random-seed procedures are missing, and runtime results omit variance and sufficiently precise hardware/batching methodology. Overall, the idea is plausible and experimentally promising, but the novelty, controls, statistical support, and evidence for the central efficiency claims are not competitive at the stated venue threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in visual world-model planning and proposes a simple, controllable mechanism for trading token count against planning quality.

The evaluation covers six simulated control environments with varied spatial and dynamics requirements. Comparisons against both full-patch and CLS-token models clearly illustrate the relevant accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

Moderate token dropping often preserves or improves success while substantially reducing measured planning time, with particularly favorable results relative to the compact CLS baseline on spatially demanding tasks.

The grouped-attention ablation, comparisons with multiple token-selection and merging strategies, probing experiments, and planning-noise study provide useful analysis beyond a basic performance table.
The presentation is generally clear, and the appendix supplies substantial architectural, dataset, and baseline-implementation detail.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the central technique combines random patch dropout with grouped attention, closely related to established patch-dropout and token-pruning ideas. The paper does not sufficiently establish why this constitutes a major conceptual advance beyond applying these mechanisms to world-model rollouts.

The success-rate results lack uncertainty estimates, independent training-seed results, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. With only 20–60 evaluation episodes and ten tested dropout ratios, highlighting the best ratios can substantially overstate improvements over the full-patch baseline.

Claims concerning real-time deployment are not supported by the reported latency: planning takes roughly 38–297 seconds per iteration. The evaluation also omits FLOPs, memory use, throughput, and a clearly specified timing protocol, making the practical efficiency implications difficult to assess.

The paper incorrectly states that computation scales exponentially with the number of visual tokens; standard self-attention scales quadratically. Several other claims use terms such as “significantly” without statistical evidence.

The mechanistic explanation is not fully convincing. The inference from a visually unstructured two-dimensional UMAP plot to approximately input-independent Gaussian prediction errors is unjustified, while the HSIC and probing analyses are largely restricted to one environment and relatively coarse state targets.

Baseline fairness and reproducibility need clarification. The paper does not fully isolate the effects of grouped-attention training from inference-time dropping, Table 3 averages over dropout ratios and contains missing entries, and no implementation for the proposed method is provided. There are also inconsistencies between the general 100-epoch training description and the dataset-specific epoch counts.

All experiments use simulation and primarily one DINO encoder, leaving real-robot behavior, alternative representations, distribution shifts, and automatic dropout-rate selection untested. Overall, the core result is promising, but the novelty and evidential rigor fall slightly below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck in transformer-based visual world-model planning with a simple, low-overhead token-subsampling approach.
The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering multiple control benchmarks, several planning paradigms, different visual encoders, VLA-guided planning, and two physical-robot tasks.
Reports useful efficiency measurements, including end-to-end planning time and a component-level latency breakdown showing that the main gains arise from reduced self-attention cost.
Includes meaningful ablations of grouped-attention training, dropout ratio, planning horizon, alternative token-selection methods, prediction quality, and adaptive sparsity.

The comparison with learned, attention-based, stratified, and clustering-based token reduction methods is informative; the blind-spot hypothesis is supported by controlled success-rate and occurrence-rate analyses.
The method is conceptually clear and produces practically relevant trade-offs: around 50% token dropout often preserves full-patch performance while materially reducing planning latency.
weaknesses: The experimental conclusions lack statistical rigor. Most simulation results provide only point estimates without confidence intervals, independent training seeds, or significance tests. Consequently, many claimed improvements or equivalences could reflect evaluation variance.

The physical-robot evidence is too small for strong claims: each task has only 10 trials, so changes such as 60% to 80% correspond to only two additional successes. Moreover, the main text says block positions were unseen during training for both tasks, whereas the appendix states that Drawer evaluates positions included in training.

The full-patch comparison appears confounded by training architecture: sparse models use randomized grouped attention, while the principal Full baseline is described as a standard DINO-WM-style model. A same-checkpoint, grouped-attention model evaluated with zero dropout is needed to isolate the effect of inference-time sparsification.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous, including the precise attention mask, whether grouping is resampled per layer or batch, how arbitrary retained-token sets and positional information are handled during autoregressive prediction, and how Equation 1 applies when only subsets interact. This limits reproducibility.

No code or trained-model release is identified, despite the reproducibility statement. Seeds, uncertainty reporting, complete per-ratio baseline results, and sufficiently precise timing protocols are also missing.

Table 4 averages success across dropout ratios, obscuring whether competing token-selection methods behave differently at practically relevant operating points. Several baseline adaptations are bespoke, and no strong dynamic, rollout-aware importance-selection baseline is evaluated.

The paper generalizes the blind-spot explanation too strongly. The evidence establishes failures for the tested mostly static selection rules, but does not justify calling this a fundamental problem of importance-based sampling generally.

Claims of real-time deployment and dramatic efficiency are overstated. At 50% dropout, average end-to-end reduction in Table 2 is about 40%, fixed encoder/environment costs remain substantial, and reported physical-robot planner latencies are still roughly 10 seconds per episode.

Architectural generalization is demonstrated only on PointMaze with single point estimates, which is insufficient to support broad claims of seamless applicability to arbitrary transformer world models.

Overall, the core idea is useful and the evaluation has promising breadth, but confounding, weak uncertainty quantification, limited real-robot evidence, and reproducibility gaps place the work slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in visual world-model planning with a simple, low-overhead token-sparsification strategy.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering six classical control environments, LIBERO-10, 50 Meta-World tasks, two physical-robot tasks, multiple visual encoders, and both sampling- and gradient-based planners.

Comparisons include several learned, attention-based, stratified-sampling, and token-merging alternatives. The latency decomposition also usefully confirms that most savings arise from reduced self-attention computation.
Ablations provide evidence that randomized grouped-attention training improves prediction under sparse inputs and that moderate sparsity can preserve aggregate task performance.
weaknesses: The central technical novelty is limited: random patch dropping and dropout-trained transformer robustness are established ideas, and the principal contribution is their adaptation to world-model rollouts. Most success-rate results lack confidence intervals, variation across seeds, or significance tests. Several claimed improvements or matches are only a few successes apart—for example, 29% versus 33% on 100 LIBERO trials and differences measured over only 10 physical trials—so the evidence does not establish statistical equivalence or improvement.

The real-world generalization description is inconsistent: the main text states that initial locations were unseen during training for both tasks, whereas the appendix says the Drawer evaluation used two positions included in training. Together with fixed scene configurations, a single selected goal, and only 10 trials per task, this substantially weakens the real-world claim.

The key Full-versus-sparse comparison appears to conflate token sparsity with training procedure: the Full baseline is described as standard full-attention DINO-WM, while the sparse system uses randomized grouped-attention training. Planning results for the same grouped-attention checkpoint evaluated with all tokens versus sparse tokens are needed to isolate the effect of sparse imagination.

The claim of enabling real-time planning is not convincingly supported. Classical-domain planning still takes tens to hundreds of seconds per iteration, while robot timings use a different asynchronous, per-episode measurement. Hardware, batching, synchronization, and end-to-end latency protocols are insufficiently specified for a fair systems conclusion.

The explanatory analyses overreach. Visual absence of structure in a 2-D UMAP projection does not justify treating prediction errors as independent zero-mean Gaussian noise; the probing experiment predicts only coarse particle-coordinate statistics; and the proposed blind-spot explanation is demonstrated mainly against static importance methods rather than strong dynamic, trajectory-aware selection.

Table 4 averages over widely different dropout ratios and tasks without uncertainty, obscuring operating-point trade-offs and making the statement that no alternative significantly outperforms random sampling unsupported.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the detailed appendix: no implementation is supplied, and important details of mask construction, positional encoding for arbitrary subsets, batching, randomness, evaluation seeds, and timing methodology remain unclear. Overall, the idea is plausible and the evaluation breadth is promising, but the novelty, statistical rigor, and control of experimental confounds fall slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper identifies an important practical bottleneck in transformer-based visual world-model planning and proposes a simple, computationally inexpensive solution: randomly sparsifying visual tokens during imagined rollouts, supported by randomized grouped-attention training.
The evaluation is unusually broad, covering six trajectory-optimization domains, LIBERO-10, 50 Meta-World tasks, two physical-robot tasks, multiple planning paradigms, and several visual encoders.

The efficiency evidence is compelling: moderate sparsity often preserves full-patch performance while materially reducing latency, and the component-level profiling confirms that most savings arise from reduced self-attention computation.

The comparison with learned, attention-based, stratified, and clustering-based token-reduction methods is valuable. The blind-spot analysis provides an intuitive and quantitatively supported explanation for why random sampling can be robust in dynamic planning.

The appendix contains substantial implementation detail and useful ablations on grouped attention, planning horizon, prediction quality, adaptive dropout, gradient-based planning, and robustness to prediction noise.
weaknesses: The core technical ingredients—random patch dropout and masked/grouped attention—are relatively incremental. The principal novelty is their application and empirical characterization in world-model planning rather than a fundamentally new modeling or planning method.

Statistical reporting is insufficient for several central claims. Most success rates lack confidence intervals or significance tests, and some apparent gains are small relative to the evaluation size, such as 29% to 33% on 100 LIBERO trials. Averaging token-selection results across sparsity levels in Table 4 also obscures variance and operating-point behavior.

The physical-robot evaluation has only 10 trials per task, so improvements such as 60% to 80% correspond to very few additional successes. There is also a protocol inconsistency: the main text says both tasks use unseen initial block locations, whereas the appendix states that Drawer is evaluated at positions included in training.

Claims concerning real-time deployment are overstated. Reported planning costs remain large in several environments, and the paper does not sufficiently characterize hardware utilization, batching, memory, end-to-end control frequency, or asynchronous-system latency to establish real-time operation generally.

The VLA-guided evaluation lacks comparisons to alternative inexpensive candidate-ranking or planning approaches. Consequently, it establishes that sparse imagination approximates the full-patch planner efficiently, but less clearly that the overall world-model planning design is the best use of the additional computation.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite extensive hyperparameter documentation: the paper does not clearly commit to releasing the method implementation, trained models, or newly collected robot data.
